talks.title: Welcome to fwd:cloudsec 2024!
talks.teaser: Aaron Zollman details Welcome to fwd:cloudsec 2024!.
talks.summary:
Overview: fwd:cloudsec organizers deliver the 2024 North America welcome address, declaring independence from co-location with re:Invent to preserve the conference's practitioner-focused community identity.

Key Topics: fwd:cloudsec's fifth year and first intentional scheduling separation from AWS re:Invent; the value of independent cloud security dialogue; commitment to open knowledge sharing; and building community for the next five years.

Technical Details: Organizers frame the scheduling change as deliberate independence, allowing open dialogue between researchers, developers, and practitioners without vendor conference dynamics influencing content or attendance.

Takeaways: Independent security conferences serve distinct community needs that vendor-adjacent events cannot fulfill. Practitioners should support communities prioritizing open dialogue over marketing.

talks.title: I'm Doing My Part! By Mapping Cloud Incidents to ATT&CK Techniques
talks.teaser: Casey Knerr examines I'm Doing My Part! By Mapping Cloud Incidents to ATT&CK Techniques.
talks.summary:
Why Map Cloud Incidents to ATT&CK

MITRE ATT&CK enterprise lead Casey Nur argues mapping threat reports to ATT&CK techniques enables a common language for sharing intelligence, spotting trends, and finding defensive gaps. ATT&CK Cloud spans IaaS, SaaS, Google Workspace, Office 365, and Azure AD (with ongoing cleanup as platforms evolve).

Three Mapping Questions

Analysts must extract atomic behaviors from prose, determine adversary goals to select tactics (often intertwined in cloud), then match techniques and sub-techniques using descriptions and keyword search. Multiple techniques may apply; perfection is less important than consistent community feedback.

Worked Example: Midnight Blizzard

Using Microsoft reporting on APT29/Midnight Blizzard, Nur isolates password spraying against a non-MFA test tenant with low-and-slow attempts to evade detection. She notes cloud mapping can feel repetitive when reports collapse to valid cloud accounts, but diverse techniques exist beyond that pattern when reports are parsed carefully.

talks.title: One Click, Six Services: Abusing The Dangerous Multi-service Orchestration Pattern
talks.teaser: Liv Matan investigates One Click, Six Services: Abusing The Dangerous Multi-service Orchestration Pattern.
talks.summary:
Hidden Cloud Dependencies

Tenable researcher Liv Matan explains how creating one GCP Cloud Function silently provisions storage buckets, Artifact Registry, Cloud Build, Cloud Run, and Eventarc triggers. This Jenga-like orchestration expands the attack surface beyond what operators see in the console.

Service Agents and Privilege Paths

Behind-the-scenes work runs under Google-managed service agents analogous to AWS service-linked roles or Azure managed identities. Second-generation Cloud Functions add complexity by combining Cloud Run and Eventarc, creating cross-service privilege-escalation opportunities such as Cloud Run access to container images.

Confused Function Vulnerability

Matan details a bounty-awarded flaw where permission to update a Cloud Function lets an attacker inject a malicious npm dependency into package.json. During deployment, Cloud Build installs it under the default Cloud Build service account, whose broad permissions can be stolen via IMDS credential exfiltration.

Defender Takeaways

GCP's mitigation lets customers choose custom service accounts for build and runtime, deprecates the legacy default Cloud Build account, and adds organization policies. Matan warns defaults remain dangerous and minimum permissions for deployment still leave residual risk across all major cloud providers.

talks.title: Forged in Fire: Forging Multi-Cloud Open Source Swiss-Army Knife
talks.teaser: Toni de la Fuente details Forged in Fire: Forging Multi-Cloud Open Source Swiss-Army Knife.
talks.summary:
Prowler's origin story

Tony deaa and Sergio Garcia from Prowler describe how a bash-based AWS audit script grew into a multi-cloud open-source security platform. They frame the core practitioner questions: what assets exist across clouds, where sensitive data lives, who has access, and how identity and resource relationships connect across accounts.

From bash to Python rewrite

The project gained traction after Black Hat EU Arsenal demos and thousands of GitHub stars. After the founder joined AWS, Prowler expanded AWS checks, then the team rewrote the tool in Python because shell portability across Linux, BSD, and macOS had become unmaintainable.

Multi-cloud Swiss army knife

Today Prowler targets consistent visibility and remediation workflows across providers, supporting automated fixes, click-ops, and scripted remediation. The talk positions open source as the right model for cloud security communities that need shared, auditable assessment tooling.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Toni de la Fuente, creator and CEO of Prowler, and Sergio Garcia, core maintainer, present the technical evolution and architectural lessons from building Prowler, a multi-cloud open-source security tool. Presented at fwd:cloudsec, the talk details how Prowler evolved from an AWS-focused Bash script into a multi-cloud Python engine supporting AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and Kubernetes with nearly 600 security checks and over 8 million downloads.

Key Topics:
- Evolution of Prowler from a 2016 Bash script into an enterprise Python platform
- Standardization of disparate multi-cloud findings using OCSF and ASFF schemas
- SDK and API inconsistencies across AWS (Boto3), Azure SDKs, GCP, and Kubernetes
- Concurrency, rate-limit throttling mitigation, and agentless compliance mapping

Technical Details:
Prowler was initiated in 2016 as a single Bash script built atop the AWS CLI to automate the CIS AWS Benchmark 1.0. To overcome operating system portability issues (such as divergent core utilities between Linux, BSD, and macOS) and manage rapid feature expansion, the tool was entirely rewritten in Python. Expanding to multi-cloud required reconciling fundamentally inconsistent cloud resource hierarchies. The maintainers adopted the Open Cybersecurity Schema Format (OCSF) and AWS Security Finding Format (ASFF) to establish a unified data contract. In this model, AWS Account IDs, Azure Subscriptions, GCP Projects, and Kubernetes Clusters are mapped to a standardized `account_uid`, while Azure locations and Kubernetes namespaces are normalized into unified regional fields.

The speakers contrast the developer experience across cloud provider SDKs and APIs. AWS provides a mature, centralized SDK (`boto3`/`botocore`) featuring built-in paginators and configurable retry options (`max_retries`) that allow Prowler to handle API throttling during concurrent, multi-threaded regional scans. AWS also publishes a global JSON file detailing service-region availability, which Prowler queries via GitHub Actions to ensure scan coverage across commercial, GovCloud, and China partitions. Conversely, Azure requires dozens of fragmented client libraries with erratic versioning, causing frequent breaking dependencies managed via Dependabot, alongside asynchronous requirements for Microsoft Graph (`aioazure`). GCP requires asynchronous execution without native client paginators, requiring manual iteration and explicit error handling for disabled service APIs.

Compliance mapping presented another major engineering hurdle. Because regulatory frameworks (CIS, PCI DSS, MITRE ATT&CK) provide high-level requirements without cloud-specific implementation details, Prowler implemented a custom JSON compliance schema. This schema maps generic compliance requirements (such as storage encryption-at-rest) directly to technical checks across S3, RDS, Azure Blob, and GCP Cloud Storage. The architecture remains entirely agentless, utilizing least-privilege, read-only audit roles (e.g., SecurityAudit in AWS) to evaluate configurations, delivering findings through CSV, JSON, and interactive Plotly Dash dashboards.

Key Takeaways:
Developing multi-cloud security tooling requires strict abstraction layers and reliance on open data schemas like OCSF to prevent vendor lock-in and decouple assessment logic from provider APIs. Security teams should perform exhaustive multi-region and multi-partition scans by default, as unmonitored secondary regions frequently harbor rogue or forgotten cloud resources. When designing high-concurrency API scanners, developers must engineer adaptive retry mechanisms with exponential backoffs and continuous dependency integration to absorb frequent cloud SDK breaking changes.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: GCPwn: A Pentesting Tool For GCP
talks.teaser: Shows how a pentester pivots through GCP service accounts and IAM impersonation paths using an open-source Python tool.
talks.summary:
GCPwn is an open-source Python tool the speaker built over several months to help penetration testers work through Google Cloud Platform environments. It was modelled on how Pacu is used for AWS. It handles application default credentials, service account keys and standalone OAuth tokens, stores them in named workspaces, and runs enumeration, exploit and unauthenticated modules.

The live demo started with a user whose email and password had leaked in a text file. After loading those credentials, the enumeration modules listed the permissions the user held, using a test-permissions option that flagged the dangerous ones. The speaker then added a service account's project manually, used an exploit module to create a key for a service account there, and enumerated its storage buckets, downloading their contents. A note in the downloaded data pointed to further projects. Enumerating service accounts and their policy bindings revealed an implicit delegation chain, and a bindings-processing module condensed those bindings into readable summaries. The final step generated an access token along that chain, letting the tester act as a production service account. A Cloud Function demo was skipped for time.

The takeaway is that chains of service account impersonation and IAM bindings can turn one weak credential into access across projects. Practitioners can follow the tool's planned wiki for its modules and flags. In Q&A, the speaker said the tool does not yet check every impersonation method, beyond paths that end in an access token.

talks.title: Trust Me Bro: Preexisting Trust is the New Initial Access Vector
talks.teaser: Shows how misconfigured IAM trust policies and an AppSync casing quirk let outsiders assume roles in victim AWS accounts.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how AWS IAM roles trust AWS services such as EC2, Lambda, and AppSync to assume them on a customer's behalf. Cross-account PassRole normally stops an outside account from attaching someone else's role to a service. The speaker argues that the pre-existing trust between a victim's role and a service can be hijacked as an initial access path, which matters as organizations retire long-lived IAM user keys.

The first case is a confused deputy flaw in AWS AppSync. The PassRole check was case sensitive in a way the service did not enforce, so changing the casing of a parameter bypassed the cross-account block. An attacker could then make AppSync assume a role in another account and invoke API calls, such as a DynamoDB scan. The second case involves Cognito identity pools and roles created by AWS Amplify. Roles whose trust policies lacked a source condition could be assumed by anyone holding a token from a Cognito identity pool using the basic flow. Amplify roles carried this flaw from 2018 until a later change removed the condition, and testing public GitHub role references revealed many vulnerable roles.

AWS has since fixed both issues, though roles that already existed stayed exposed until owners changed them. Defenders should audit trust policies for service principals, add source account, source ARN, or organization conditions where they work, and review Cognito identity pools with the basic flow enabled. Service control policies can add an account-wide guardrail, but they should be tested carefully before production use.

talks.title: Open-Sourcing AWS Pentest Methodology
talks.teaser: Proposes an open AWS pentest methodology built around gathering context, mapping attack paths and testing multi-account setups.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why AWS penetration testing needs a shared, community-accepted methodology. The speaker reviews two existing resources: a 2019 Cloud Security Alliance framework built on STRIDE, which describes some cloud concepts oddly and assumes a single account, and a community wiki with service-specific guides that is hard to keep current. Neither addresses AWS Organizations or service control policies well.

The methodology described starts with meetings with the client, including one-on-one conversations, and a review of diagrams and documentation. With white-box access, the tester uses visualization tools and automated checks such as Scout Suite and Prowler, while noting that some services lack coverage. Manual work follows in layers: reviewing each service on its own, then how services depend on one another, then how accounts relate through Organizations, trust policies and service control policies. Each candidate attack path is treated as a hypothesis and confirmed or disproved through testing from an assumed-breach position.

Recommendations should be practical and preventive, such as a control that stops IAM users from being created where the client's context allows it. The speaker names limitations, including the time needed at scale, the difficulty of keeping notes, and "scan and rebrand" vendors who pass automated reports off as full pentests. The speaker asks practitioners to help write, review and host an open-source version of the framework.

talks.title: The EKS Hacking Playbook: Lessons From 3 Years of Cloud Security Research
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers move from one EKS pod to AWS credentials, exposed EFS shares and other tenants through misconfigurations.
talks.summary:
The speakers, security researchers on a cloud research team, open with a short primer on Kubernetes concepts such as containers, pods, nodes and clusters, then explain why Amazon EKS creates its own security questions, since it combines Kubernetes practices with AWS ones. Their first focus is EKS Pod Identity. The node-level agent maps a pod's Kubernetes identity to AWS credentials over plain HTTP, so any attacker who can run a pod in the same network namespace can sniff both the Kubernetes token and the returned AWS credentials.

The middle of the talk covers registry and storage exposure. Image pull secrets, obtained through the ECR login command, can be used to pull images from the internal registry. In a case study on an Alibaba Cloud database service, the credentials granted push rights as well, which would allow a supply-chain attack, and the registry was shared with other internal services. The speakers then turn to EFS file shares. In a dataset of tens of thousands of shares, about 85% had no access policy, and roughly 93% overall could be reached without authentication. In an undisclosed case at a large cloud company, a network-isolated pod bypassed a firewall and found EFS shares holding customer files, with the disclosure still in progress.

The final section looks at the instance metadata service. A pod that can reach the node's metadata endpoint can fetch the node's identity and use it against the Kubernetes API, exposing other pods and secrets. In a Hugging Face engagement, a malicious model gave code execution inside a pod, which led to access across customer environments. The bugs have since been fixed. The speakers stress that these issues are misconfigurations and can be prevented, with a metadata hop limit suggested as a mitigation. Their takeaway is that EKS must be reviewed through both the Kubernetes and AWS layers.

talks.title: From Intrusion to Insight: Lessons learned from of a month long AWS compromise
talks.teaser: Walks through a month-long AWS account compromise, from a leaked access key to email abuse, with lessons for cloud responders.
talks.summary:
The talk recounts an AWS incident response case in which an attacker got in with a long-term access key that had been exposed, most likely through environment variables, build scripts or container images, although some evidence was already gone and the exact source could not be confirmed. The key carried administrator permissions, so the intruder created IAM users with console logins, extra access keys and policies, plus a small EC2 instance whose security group allowed inbound RDP. That backdoor meant removing the original key did not end the access.

The attacker then turned to Amazon SES to send mail and check sending quotas, and used Route 53 to host domains that imitated a payment brand. Further discovery covered Pinpoint SMS, SNS and RDS snapshots. A cross-account IAM role trusting an external AWS account gave another persistent path, and the intruder checked permissions with the IAM policy simulator, a technique that matched the CloudFox tool. A large machine learning instance was denied by a vCPU quota, and a Lightsail launch was blocked pending account verification. The case ended when repeated support requests to raise SES limits made AWS suspicious and it contacted the customer's technical account manager.

For responders, the lessons include deactivating credentials instead of deleting them, avoiding premature removal of VMs that may hold evidence, and centralising logs in advance. Athena can query CloudTrail and flow logs quickly, while budget alerts, IAM Access Analyzer and premium logging help catch misuse early. Billing spikes can also reveal data exfiltration. The speaker cautioned against leaving response entirely to an IT provider and against blaming developers for long-lived keys.
